title: Project Volga
intro: The online bookstore I built across two semesters, starting right after Computer Science I.
story: In Web Concepts I, I built the storefront visitors would see. In Web Concepts II, I connected it to the back end. I named it after a river in the tradition of another online bookstore. Watching the two halves finally work together is one of my favorite memories from those courses.

images.caption: Original bookstore
images.alt: The Volga Book Store homepage with book covers, a category menu, and the shopping cart.

teaching.label: How I teach Computer Science I

detail.title: Following a book through the store
detail.body: The page shows book jackets, a category list, and a cart. In the first semester I could lay those out and make the store look convincing. In the second semester I had to make sure the book a shopper selected in the catalog was the one that appeared in the cart. It is still an example I can show students who wonder where their first programming course might lead.

title: On the Radar
intro: A course-planning prototype that uses a radar chart to show which requirements a student’s course choices cover.
story: I worked on the team that built the Vue version for students, advisors, and department administrators. We used MongoDB, Express, Vue, and Node.js. A later team continued the project in Angular. These screenshots preserve the version our team worked on.

images.caption: Academic planning view
images.alt: Desktop dashboard showing a radar chart next to the course-planning controls.

images.caption: Add a course
images.alt: Mobile form with fields for adding a course to the planner.

images.caption: Course list
images.alt: Mobile course list with expandable rows for individual courses.

images.caption: Edit an account
images.alt: Mobile account-editing dialog over the planning application.

detail.title: One plan, several viewpoints
detail.body: A list can tell a student which courses they picked. The radar chart was our way of showing which general education requirements those choices covered. The small-screen views show how an administrator could enter courses and maintain accounts behind the planning dashboard.

title: Mission Got Your Six
intro: A community website for a veteran-led organization supporting veterans and first responders.
story: Nick needed a domain, hosting, and a website to tell people about the mission. I volunteered in 2018, and former classmates helped build the site. It launched in June 2019. I have continued to donate the hosting, domain, and time to maintain it.

images.caption: Original homepage
images.alt: Mission Got Your Six homepage featuring the organization’s name and a parachutist in flight.

images.caption: Original site design
images.alt: An interior view of the early site with its navigation and military imagery.

detail.title: Keeping a community project online
detail.body: I met Nick’s project as a student intern at the App Factory. His fundraising and events brought veterans and first responders together, and the site gave people a way to find that work. Former classmates built the first version, and more people joined in 2021. Maintaining the domain and hosting has let the project outlast any one student team.

title: CCSC Midwest conferences
intro: Three editions of the Midwest computing conference website, from 2018 through 2020.
story: In spring 2018 I took on the first site for the Consortium for Computing Sciences in Colleges Midwest conference. Our work continued across three events. Each edition brought together the program, calls for papers, registration, and directions for a different host campus.

images.caption: 2018 conference
images.alt: The 2018 Midwest Conference homepage with a campus photograph behind the conference title.

images.caption: 2019 conference
images.alt: The 2019 conference homepage featuring Benedictine University.

images.caption: 2020 conference
images.alt: The 2020 Midwest Conference header and calls for submissions.

detail.title: A website that changes with its host
detail.body: Dr. Zaid Altahat assigned me the first conference build in spring 2018. The host campus and dates changed each year. Someone submitting a paper needed a different set of details from someone looking for a workshop or directions on arrival. The three screenshots show how the conference website handled those recurring jobs across successive editions.

title: Nature’s Best Shea Butter
intro: An early MIS team project building a storefront for a local entrepreneur.
story: Our MIS 220 team worked with a client who needed a place to present her shea butter products. We organized her catalog in Weebly. It was one of my first chances to design around what a real business owner needed. I now bring community projects into Systems Analysis and Design.

images.caption: Original storefront
images.alt: Nature’s Best Online Store with a shea butter product photograph and the founder’s introduction.

teaching.label: How I teach Systems Analysis and Design

detail.title: Making a catalog work for its owner
detail.body: Our assignment was to give the entrepreneur a storefront that could hold her product line. The homepage put the founder’s introduction next to a photograph of her shea butter. Years later, when I teach systems analysis, I ask students to find out what the person who will run the business needs the system to do.

title: Anne Morse-Hambrock
intro: A portfolio and music storefront for a harpist, writer, humorist, and performer.
story: The project brought several parts of Anne’s work into one site. Visitors could explore her music, buy recordings, and inquire about performances. The screenshots show the design I worked on, and the link leads to her current website.

images.caption: Artist homepage
images.alt: Anne Morse-Hambrock’s original homepage with a harp beside her name.

images.caption: Music catalog
images.alt: A grid of Anne’s recordings in the original online music catalog.

detail.title: Buying an album or booking a performance
detail.body: Someone who wanted to hear Anne play the harp could browse albums and individual tracks. A couple planning a wedding or an organizer booking a speaker needed a booking path, including payments and deposits. The homepage and catalog show how those different reasons for visiting fit under one artist’s name.

title: The App Factory website
intro: An undergraduate software engineering project documenting apps built by student development teams.
story: The site began in Software Engineering I and II. We used WordPress on a Linux, Apache, MySQL, and PHP stack in an Amazon EC2 instance. The archive includes project screenshots and profiles of the people who worked on them.

images.caption: Team website
images.alt: The archived App Factory homepage with student team members and project navigation.

detail.title: Putting student software on the web
detail.body: A visitor could look at an app screenshot and then see the student programmers and designers behind it. Building that record gave our Software Engineering team a concrete hosting assignment, too. The application and database ran on a Linux server in Amazon EC2, so delivering a WordPress site also meant making the underlying services work together.

title: Professional DJ Store
intro: One of the first online stores I designed for a Milwaukee sound and lighting business.
story: Custom Designed Lighting, Sound & Video supplied the clubs and venues where this gear went to work. This storefront predates my formal UX training. The script logo, drop shadows, and dense product listings are part of why I kept it. They make a good starting point for a conversation about how web design has changed.

images.caption: Store homepage
images.alt: The early DJ storefront uses a script masthead and columns of lighting and sound equipment.

images.caption: Equipment catalog
images.alt: The original catalog view with product photographs, prices, and cart buttons.

detail.title: From a Bay View counter to an online catalog
detail.body: Custom Designed Lighting, Sound & Video was a Milwaukee business that designed and installed equipment for clubs and sports bars. The online shop grew out of its Bay View storefront. I knew what the gear did in a room; the design challenge was explaining the same equipment to someone who could only see a photograph and a price.

title: DJ Tonya’s mix archive
intro: My collection of music video mixes, mixtapes, and footage from the DJ booth.
story: I started working as a DJ in 1980 and still make new video mixes. This site gives the recordings a home. The screenshot preserves an earlier design, while the current archive brings together mixes and footage from La Cage and Milwaukee PrideFest.

links.label: Read the Wisconsin LGBTQ History Project interview

images.caption: Earlier archive design
images.alt: An earlier DJ Tonya homepage with a concert crowd and stage lights across the header.

detail.title: Preserving a piece of Milwaukee music history
detail.body: The recordings have a history outside the website. I spent two decades as the house DJ at La Cage, and the archive includes work from Milwaukee PrideFest. In August 2026, Michail Takach wrote about that part of my life for the Wisconsin LGBTQ History Project. The interview gives the mixes a time, a place, and a dance floor.

title: Barnacle Bud’s
intro: A hand-coded restaurant website with original artwork and icons for a web design course.
story: Our Art 377 brief asked us to redesign an independent restaurant’s website. I chose a friend’s restaurant in Bay View. I made the artwork and icons by hand and wrote the HTML and CSS for the site.

images.caption: Restaurant design
images.alt: The restaurant design pairs a waterside photograph with a menu and food photography.

detail.title: Designing for someone choosing a restaurant
detail.body: The waterfront setting gave me a starting point, but a visitor also needed to find the menu. The archived homepage shows how I used the waterside photograph, food images, and hand-drawn navigation to put those two tasks together. Writing the HTML and CSS myself let me place each piece of artwork where it belonged.

title: Gear Blabs
intro: My first WordPress blog, built around the sound and lighting equipment I knew from live shows.
story: For Art 477, I had to design a blog to a set of specifications. I used sound systems, stage lighting, and shows as the subject. That gave me a familiar collection of material to organize while learning a new publishing tool.

images.caption: Blog homepage
images.alt: Gear Blabs homepage with live-stage photography behind an audio and lighting article.

detail.title: Giving a blog a subject I knew
detail.body: I could draw on the lighting rigs, audio equipment, and performances I already knew from live production. The brief was a mock blog for Art 477, so the point was to learn how a publishing system handles successive articles and images. A photograph of a show could lead into a post about the equipment that made it possible.

title: Rainbow of Dreams Gifts
intro: A WordPress and WooCommerce storefront for a Racine gift and craft-fair business.
story: Pat and Patrick Shay sold gifts at regional shows. The website gave their products a browsable catalog and online storefront. In 2021, the owners joined their business with the Racine Marian Center. This screenshot preserves the earlier shop.

images.caption: Gift catalog
images.alt: The archived Rainbow of Dreams storefront with photographs of gifts arranged in a product grid.

detail.title: A second storefront for a craft-fair business
detail.body: At a show, shoppers see items side by side and can ask the owners what they are looking at. Online, the product photos and catalog had to do more of that work. WordPress handled the pages and WooCommerce supplied the shopping tools. The archived grid shows the business before its move into a brick-and-mortar partnership.

title: Chi Steppin
intro: An event website for a weekend of Chicago-style stepping and dance instruction.
story: The organizers needed one place to explain the event, introduce the dance lessons, and share weekend details with attendees. The original design is preserved here.

images.caption: Event homepage
images.alt: The Chi Steppin event homepage with a bright navigation bar and venue photographs.

detail.title: What a first-time attendee needed to know
detail.body: The weekend brought professional dance instruction and a private event together. People planning to attend needed to understand the style of dance, find the venue, and know that buying a ticket in advance was recommended. Those practical questions gave the event pages their structure.

title: Save the Tigers!
intro: A conservation website with original visual assets, written from scratch in HTML and CSS.
story: For this Art 377 project, I researched the Bengal tiger and turned the findings into a short educational website. I made the graphics in Illustrator and Photoshop, then implemented the design by hand.

images.caption: Conservation website
images.alt: The Bengal Tiger Foundation class project with tiger photographs and illustrated navigation.

detail.title: Turning research into a small public site
detail.body: The brief called for four or five pages about an endangered species. After researching Bengal tigers, I used Illustrator and Photoshop to make a consistent set of visual elements and built the pages in HTML and CSS. The illustrated navigation helped carry a reader from the opening photograph into the subject.
